epic.name: Bulk approval and a self-updating list
unverifiedAssumptions: Verify that approving cannot overturn a colleague's rejection: the app assumes the service refuses (or harmlessly ignores) an approve call for a request that is already Rejected, and it only guards against that by checking each request's state a moment before sending. The written contract for the approve call says only that it 'sets the Status to Approved', with no mention of a guard. If it really does overwrite, a bulk approval could silently flip a rejection your colleague recorded seconds earlier — and nothing on screen would say so.

Verify the result counts match reality: the report of 'how many approved, how many left unchanged' is worked out by re-reading the list immediately after the approvals are sent. If the service takes a moment to reflect them, the report could tell you 0 approved when everything in fact worked. Approve a handful, note the numbers you are told, then reload the page and count the Approved rows — they should agree.

Verify a 15-second refresh is comfortable against your real data volumes: the list re-reads every request each time (the service offers no way to ask for just what changed), and this was only ever exercised against small test data. On a batch near the 10,000-request ceiling you may notice the screen stutter every 15 seconds or the refresh not finishing before the next one is due.

Confirm the exact shape of the single-request approve call, its confirmation composition and its staleness re-check against the merged main once expense-decisions lands. This epic was planned while that epic was still building, so those three reuse points were planned from its story files rather than observed in code — the story files mark them as dependency seams to check before building.
